quiz.why: Track `farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])`. A 0 only blocks you if nothing earlier can jump past it.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Jump Game**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Jump Game**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

quiz.q: Since the input is already sorted, insertion takes…
options: One linear pass: before, overlapping (merge), after
A binary search for the spot, then an O(1) insert
Pushing every interval into a heap by start
quiz.why: That takes O(n) time. Binary search finds the spot, but merging and shifting are still O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Insert Interval**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Insert Interval**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n) for the output.

quiz.q: After sorting by start, an interval overlaps the last merged one when…
quiz.why: Touching endpoints count as overlapping here.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Merge Intervals**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n log n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Merge Intervals**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: Which interval should you keep when two overlap?
quiz.why: An earlier end leaves the most room for the rest.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Non-overlapping Intervals**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n log n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Non-overlapping Intervals**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1) beyond sorting.

quiz.q: What does the min-heap of end times represent?
options: The rooms in use, with the soonest-free room on top
The rooms in use, with the latest-free room on top
Start times of the meetings still waiting for a room
quiz.why: The heap's final size is the peak number of concurrent meetings.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Meeting Rooms II**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n log n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Meeting Rooms II**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: How do you rotate a matrix 90° clockwise in place?
options: Transpose, then reverse the order of the rows
Reverse each row, then reverse each column
quiz.why: Check it on a 2×2 example. The two middle options rotate counter-clockwise, and the last one rotates 180°.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Rotate Image**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n²).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Rotate Image**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

quiz.q: Why re-check `top <= bottom` before walking the bottom row?
options: A single remaining row would otherwise be visited twice
Without it, the corner cells would be skipped
top can run past the last index of the matrix
The loop would otherwise stop one row early
quiz.why: The same goes for `left <= right` with a single column.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Spiral Matrix**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(m · n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Spiral Matrix**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1) besides the output.

quiz.q: How does the O(1)-space version remember which rows and columns to zero?
options: It uses the first row and first column as marker storage
It zeroes each row at once and the columns afterwards
It scans the matrix twice without storing anything
It copies the matrix and reads the zeros from the copy
quiz.why: Track row 0 separately, because it doubles as a marker row.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Set Matrix Zeroes**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(m · n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Set Matrix Zeroes**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

quiz.q: In bitwise addition, `(a & b) << 1` is…
options: The bits where a and b differ
quiz.why: `a ^ b` adds without carrying; repeat until the carry is 0.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Sum of Two Integers**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(32).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Sum of Two Integers**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(1).

quiz.q: When do you shrink the window from the left?
options: While it still contains all the required characters
Whenever it grows longer than t, to keep it short
Whenever a character in the window repeats
Only once `right` has reached the end of s
quiz.why: Keep shrinking while it is still valid, recording the best window as you go.

quiz.q: Why push `(val, i, node)` into the heap instead of `(val, node)`?
options: Ties on val would compare ListNodes, which raises TypeError
So nodes from the same list keep their original order
Because heapq orders tuples by their last item first
Because ListNodes can't be hashed without an index
quiz.why: The unique index i breaks ties before Python ever compares nodes.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Merge K Sorted Lists**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(N log k).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Merge K Sorted Lists**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(k).

quiz.q: What does the recursive helper return to its parent?
options: The best downward path from this node, using one branch
The best path through this node, using both branches
The best path anywhere inside this node's subtree
The sum of every value in this node's subtree
quiz.why: A path passing up through the parent can only continue down one side. The both-branches path is used to update the global best, not returned.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(h).

quiz.q: Why include null markers ('N') when serializing?
options: Without them, different shapes could produce the same string
They mark where each level ends for the decoder
They keep the string length equal to the node count
They let the decoder skip values it has already seen
quiz.why: Preorder plus null markers determines the tree exactly.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is O(n) for both.

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: Why build a trie of the words instead of searching for each word separately?
options: One DFS per cell explores all words at once, pruning dead prefixes
A trie stores the words in less memory than a list
It stops a single word from reusing a grid cell
So the found words come out in sorted order
quiz.why: Searching word by word repeats the same grid exploration for every word. Reusing cells is prevented by marking, not by the trie.

quiz.q: What do the two heaps hold?
options: Max-heap of the lower half, min-heap of the upper half
Min-heap of the lower half, max-heap of the upper half
A max-heap and a min-heap of all values
One heap of even values and one heap of odd values
quiz.why: The median sits at the heap tops: the largest of the lower half and the smallest of the upper half.

quiz.q: What is the **time complexity** of the optimal solution to **Find Median from Data Stream**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's time complexity is `add_num` O(log n), `find_median` O(1).

quiz.q: What is the **space complexity** of the optimal solution to **Find Median from Data Stream**?
quiz.why: The optimal solution's space complexity is O(n).

quiz.q: What does one adjacent word pair tell you?
options: The first differing characters give one ordering edge
Every position where they differ gives an ordering edge
Their first characters give one ordering edge
Nothing, unless both words have the same length
quiz.why: Characters after the first difference carry no information, and equal first characters say nothing.

problems.title: One Less
problems.desc:
Given a whole number `n`, return the number that comes **just before** it.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: Your function receives a number called `n`. Whatever comes after the word `return` is what the function hands back as its answer.
The number just before another one is that number minus one. Python uses `-` for subtraction.
Write `return` followed by a calculation that uses `n`. Check it on the example: for 5 you should get 4.
problems.solution:
def one_less(n: int) -> int:
    return n - 1

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Return a value:** `return something` sends `something` back as the answer.
**Indentation:** the `return` line sits 4 spaces in from `def`.

problems.title: Double It
problems.desc:
Return twice the value of `n`.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: "Twice" a number means the number multiplied by 2.
Python's multiplication sign is `*` (not `x` or `×`).
Return the calculation in one line. For 3 you should get 6, and for 0 you should get 0.
problems.solution:
def double(n: int) -> int:
    return n * 2

problems.title: Rectangle Area
problems.desc:
Return the area of a rectangle that is `width` wide and `height` tall (width × height).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= width, height <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def area(width: int, height: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: The area of a rectangle is its width multiplied by its height.
Both values arrive as the function's inputs (its parameters), so you can use their names directly in a calculation.
Return the product of the two parameters using `*`.
problems.solution:
def area(width: int, height: int) -> int:
    return width * height

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Two parameters:** use both names, `width` and `height`, directly.

problems.title: Change Due
problems.desc:
You buy `items` things that each cost `price`, and hand over `paid`. Return the change you get back.

You always pay enough.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= price, items <= 1000`
- `0 <= paid <= 10^5`
- `paid >= price * items`
problems.starter:
def change_due(price: int, paid: int, items: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: First work out what you spent in total, then take that away from what you paid.
The total cost is the price of one item times how many items you bought.
Python does `*` before `-` (just like in maths), so you can write the whole thing in one expression. Add brackets if it makes it clearer to you.
problems.solution:
def change_due(price: int, paid: int, items: int) -> int:
    return paid - price * items

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Order of operations:** `*` and `/` happen before `+` and `-`, so `paid - price * items` multiplies first.
**Brackets:** `(price * items)` makes the order obvious, if you prefer.
**A variable for a step:** `acc = cost * elems` then `return handed - acc`.

problems.title: Average of Two
problems.desc:
Return the average of `a` and `b` as a **float** (a number with a decimal point).

**Constraints**
- `-1000 <= a, b <= 1000`
problems.starter:
def average(a: int, b: int) -> float:
    pass
hints: The average of two numbers is their total divided by 2.
In Python, `/` always gives a float (a number with a decimal point), which is exactly what's asked for.
Add the numbers first and then divide. Without brackets, Python divides only the second number, because `/` happens before `+`.
problems.solution:
def average(a: int, b: int) -> float:
    return (a + b) / 2

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **True division:** `/` always gives a float: `4 / 2` is `2.0`.
**Brackets first:** `(a + b) / 2`. Without them, only `b` is divided.
**This task checks the type:** returning `3` instead of `3.0` counts as wrong.

problems.title: Share the Sweets
problems.desc:
Share `sweets` equally between `kids`, giving each child as many **whole** sweets as possible. Return a list `[each, left_over]`: how many each child gets, and how many are left.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= sweets <= 10^16`
- `1 <= kids <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def share(sweets: int, kids: int) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: Two different questions: how many whole sweets each child gets, and how many are left over.
`//` divides and throws away the remainder (whole-number division). `%` gives just the remainder.
Return a list with both answers inside square brackets, in the order `[each, left_over]`. For 7 sweets and 2 kids that's `[3, 1]`.
problems.solution:
def share(sweets: int, kids: int) -> List[int]:
    return [sweets // kids, sweets % kids]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Return a list of two values:** `return [first, second]`

problems.title: Is It Even?
problems.desc:
Return `True` if `n` is even, otherwise `False`.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: A number is even when dividing it by 2 leaves nothing over.
`%` gives the remainder after division, and `==` checks whether two values are equal. A comparison is already `True` or `False`.
Return the comparison directly; you don't need an `if`. Remember 0 is even too.
problems.solution:
def is_even(n: int) -> bool:
    return n % 2 == 0

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Remainder:** `n % 2` is `0` for even numbers and `1` for odd ones.
**Compare:** `==` gives `True` or `False`, so you can return a comparison directly.

problems.title: Power Of
problems.desc:
Return `base` raised to the power `exp`.

**Constraints**
- `-100 <= base <= 100`
- `0 <= exp <= 100`
problems.starter:
def power(base: int, exp: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: "Raised to the power" means multiplying the base by itself `exp` times. For example, 2 to the power 3 is 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
Python has a power operator: two stars, `**`.
Anything to the power 0 is 1, and the operator already handles that for you.
problems.solution:
def power(base: int, exp: int) -> int:
    return base ** exp

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Power:** `base ** exp`. (`^` is *not* power in Python; it's a bit operation.)

problems.title: Can Vote
problems.desc:
People can vote from age 18. Return `True` if someone aged `age` can vote.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= age <= 150`
hints: You need a yes/no answer, which in Python is `True` or `False`.
A comparison like `x > 5` already produces `True` or `False`, so you can return it directly.
Be careful at exactly 18: someone aged 18 *can* vote, so use "greater than or equal to", which is `>=`.
problems.solution:
def can_vote(age: int) -> bool:
    return age >= 18

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Return the comparison itself:** `return years >= 18` already is `True` or `False`.

problems.title: Different Values
problems.desc:
Return `True` if `a` and `b` are different numbers.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= a, b <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def different(a: int, b: int) -> bool:
    pass
hints: You're asking "are these two numbers different?", and the answer is `True` or `False`.
Python's "not equal" operator is `!=` (an exclamation mark followed by an equals sign).
Return the comparison itself; no `if` is needed.
problems.solution:
def different(a: int, b: int) -> bool:
    return a != b

problems.title: Truthy or Falsy
problems.desc:
Return what `bool` says about `n`: `False` for `0`, `True` for any other number.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: Python treats every number as "true-ish" or "false-ish" (truthy or falsy): 0 counts as false, and any other number counts as true.
The built-in function `bool(...)` turns a value into exactly `True` or `False` using that rule.
Return the result of calling it on `n`. Negative numbers are truthy too.
problems.solution:
def is_truthy(n: int) -> bool:
    return bool(n)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Convert to True/False:** `bool(n)` is `False` only for zero.

problems.title: Sign of a Number
problems.desc:
Return `1` if `n` is positive, `-1` if it's negative, and `0` if it's zero.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: There are three cases (positive, negative, zero), and each one returns a different number.
`if` checks the first condition, `elif` ("else if") checks the next one, and `else` catches everything left over.
Check `n > 0` first, then `n < 0`; whatever is left must be zero. Note that 0 is neither positive nor negative.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Colons and indentation:** each condition line ends with `:`, and its block is indented 4 more spaces.
**Return inside a branch:** `return 1` ends the function right there.

problems.title: Letter Grade
problems.desc:
Turn a test `score` into a letter: 90 and above is `"A"`, 80–89 `"B"`, 70–79 `"C"`, and anything lower `"F"`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= score <= 100`
hints: Check the grades from the top down: once a score is 90 or more you know it's an A, and you don't need to check anything else.
Use `if` for the first band and `elif` for the following ones. Each branch returns its letter, which is text in quotes.
Because you check from the top, the B test only needs `score >= 80`: anything 90 or more was already caught by the A test. Mind the edges: exactly 90 is an A, exactly 80 a B.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Several cases:** one `if`, then as many `elif` as you need.
**Order matters:** check `score >= 90` before `score >= 80`, since 95 is also `>= 80`.
**Fallback:** a final `return "F"` (or an `else:`) catches everything else.

problems.title: FizzBuzz (One Number)
problems.desc:
Return `"FizzBuzz"` if `n` is divisible by both 3 and 5, `"Fizz"` if only by 3, `"Buzz"` if only by 5, and otherwise `n` as text.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: "Divisible by 3" means dividing by 3 leaves no remainder, so `n % 3 == 0`.
Order matters. Check "divisible by both" first, because 15 is also divisible by 3 and by 5 on its own. (Divisible by both 3 and 5 is the same as divisible by 15.)
If none of the checks match, return the number as text. `str(...)` turns a number into a string.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Both at once:** `n % 3 == 0 and n % 5 == 0`, or simply `n % 15 == 0`.
**Most specific first:** check FizzBuzz before Fizz and Buzz.

problems.title: In Range
problems.desc:
Return `True` if `x` is between `lo` and `hi`, **including** both ends.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= x, lo, hi <= 10^16`
- `lo <= hi`
problems.starter:
def in_range(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> bool:
    pass
hints: "Between `lo` and `hi`, including both ends" means `x` is at least `lo` AND at most `hi`.
You can join two comparisons with `and`. Python also lets you chain them like maths: `a <= b <= c`.
Use `<=` (not `<`) on both sides, so the ends themselves count.
problems.solution:
def in_range(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> bool:
    return lo <= x <= hi

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Chained shortcut:** `lo <= x <= hi` means the same thing.

problems.title: Is It the Weekend?
problems.desc:
Days are numbered 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday). Return `True` for Saturday (6) or Sunday (7).

**Constraints**
- `1 <= day <= 7`
hints: The weekend is day 6 or day 7. Any other day isn't.
`or` is `True` when at least one side is `True`.
Compare `day` with each weekend number using `==` and join the two comparisons with `or`. (Writing `day == 6 or 7` is a common mistake: the `7` on its own is always truthy.)
problems.solution:
def is_weekend(day: int) -> bool:
    return day == 6 or day == 7

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Either one:** `or`. Each side needs its own full comparison: `x == 1 or x == 2`, never `x == 1 or 2`.

problems.title: Exactly One
problems.desc:
Return `True` if exactly one of `a` and `b` is `True` (not both, not neither).

**Constraints**
- `a` and `b` are each `True` or `False`
problems.starter:
def exactly_one(a: bool, b: bool) -> bool:
    pass
hints: There are four combinations of two booleans. You want `True` only for (True, False) and (False, True).
Put another way: at least one is true (`or`), and they're not both true (`not` combined with `and`).
Combine those two ideas with `and`. Use brackets so Python groups them the way you mean.
problems.solution:
def exactly_one(a: bool, b: bool) -> bool:
    return (a or b) and not (a and b)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Group with brackets:** `(p or q)` is worked out before whatever is outside the brackets.
**Shortcut you'll see later:** `a != b` gives the same answer for bools.

problems.title: Add One to Text
problems.desc:
You get a whole number written as text. Return that number plus one, as an **int**.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(text) <= 20`
- `text` is digits, with an optional `-` in front
hints: The input is text (a string), and you can't add 1 to text: `"41" + 1` is an error.
`int(...)` turns text made of digits into a whole number.
Convert first, then add one, and return the number (not text).
problems.solution:
def add_one(text: str) -> int:
    return int(text) + 1

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Then add:** `int(text) + 1`. Adding `1` to the text itself is an error.

problems.title: Number to Text
problems.desc:
Return the number `n` written as text.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: You need the same digits, but as text (a string) instead of a number.
`str(...)` turns any value into its text form.
Return the result of calling `str` on `n`. Negative numbers keep their minus sign.
problems.solution:
def to_text(n: int) -> str:
    return str(n)

problems.title: Chop the Decimals
problems.desc:
Return `x` with everything after the decimal point removed, as an int.

**Constraints**
- `-10^10 <= x <= 10^10`
hints: You want to drop everything after the decimal point, without rounding up or down.
`int(...)` on a float does exactly that: it cuts the decimals off (truncation, towards zero).
That's why `-2.7` becomes `-2`, not `-3`. `round` would give a different answer, so don't use it here.
problems.solution:
def chop(x: float) -> int:
    return int(x)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Float to int:** `int(x)` drops the decimals, moving toward zero (so `-2.7` → `-2`).
**Not the same as `//`:** `-2.7 // 1` is `-3.0`, which rounds down instead.

problems.title: Decimal Text Doubled
problems.desc:
You get a decimal number written as text. Return twice its value as a float.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(text) <= 20`
- `text` is digits with an optional `-` in front and an optional decimal point
hints: The input is text that looks like a decimal number, such as `"2.5"`.
`float(...)` turns that text into a decimal number you can do maths with. (`int` would fail, because of the decimal point.)
Convert it first, then multiply by 2, and return the float.
problems.solution:
def doubled(text: str) -> float:
    return float(text) * 2

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Float times int is a float:** `2.5 * 2` is `5.0`.

problems.title: Distance Apart
problems.desc:
Return how far apart `a` and `b` are on the number line (always zero or positive).

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= a, b <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def distance(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: The distance between two numbers is their difference, but distance is never negative.
`abs(...)` (absolute value) removes a minus sign: `abs(-4)` is `4`.
Subtract one number from the other and wrap the result in `abs`. Then the order you subtract in doesn't matter.
problems.solution:
def distance(a: int, b: int) -> int:
    return abs(a - b)

problems.title: Round the Price
problems.desc:
Return `x` rounded to 2 decimal places.

**Constraints**
- `-10^10 <= x <= 10^10`
hints: Prices have two decimal places, so round to 2 places.
`round(value, digits)` rounds to that many decimal places. With only one argument it rounds to a whole number, which isn't what you want here.
Pass `x` and the number of decimal places, and return the result.
problems.solution:
def round_price(x: float) -> float:
    return round(x, 2)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Round to places:** `round(x, 2)`. The second argument is the number of decimal places.

problems.title: Largest of Three
problems.desc:
Return the largest of the three numbers.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= a, b, c <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def largest(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: You need whichever of the three numbers is biggest.
`max(...)` accepts as many numbers as you like, separated by commas, and returns the largest.
One call with all three inputs is enough. Negative numbers work too.
problems.solution:
def largest(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> int:
    return max(a, b, c)

problems.title: Clamp
problems.desc:
Return `x`, but forced into the range `lo`…`hi`: if it's below `lo` return `lo`, if it's above `hi` return `hi`.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= x, lo, hi <= 10^16`
- `lo <= hi`
problems.starter:
def clamp(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    pass
hints: Two limits: the answer can't go above `hi`, and it can't go below `lo`.
`min(x, hi)` keeps a number from going above `hi` (it picks the smaller of the two). `max(..., lo)` keeps it from going below `lo`.
Apply one limit, then apply the other to that result, by putting one call inside the other. Test all three cases: below, inside and above the range.
problems.solution:
def clamp(x: int, lo: int, hi: int) -> int:
    return max(lo, min(x, hi))

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Nest calls:** `max(lo, min(x, hi))`. The inner call runs first.

problems.title: Say Hello
problems.desc:
Print `Hello, NAME!` using the given `name`.

_This task checks what you **print**, not what you return._

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(name) <= 10^4`
hints: This task checks what you *print* on the screen, not what you return.
`print(...)` shows text. You can join pieces of text with `+`: the greeting, the name, then the exclamation mark.
Watch the exact output: `Hello, ` has a comma and a space after it, and the `!` comes straight after the name with no space.
problems.solution:
def greet(name: str) -> None:
    print("Hello, " + name + "!")

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Join text pieces:** `"Hello, " + name + "!"` (`+` on strings glues them).
**Why not `print("Hello,", name, "!")`?** Commas add spaces, giving `Hello, Ada !`.

problems.title: Two Lines
problems.desc:
Print `a` on one line and `b` on the next line.

_This task checks what you print._

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(a), len(b) <= 10^4`
problems.starter:
def two_lines(a: str, b: str) -> None:
    pass
hints: Each `print` call finishes with a new line automatically.
So printing one thing and then printing the other puts them on separate lines.
Use two `print` calls, `a` first and then `b`.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **One `print` per line:** each `print` ends with a new line.

problems.title: Dashed Numbers
problems.desc:
Print the three numbers on one line with dashes between them.

_This task checks what you print._

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= a, b, c <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def dashed(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> None:
    pass
hints: When you give `print` several values separated by commas, it puts a space between them by default.
The `sep=` option changes what goes between the values, for example `sep="*"`.
Print all three numbers in one call and set the separator to a dash.
problems.solution:
def dashed(a: int, b: int, c: int) -> None:
    print(a, b, c, sep="-")

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Several values:** `print(a, b, c)` puts spaces between them.

problems.title: Same Line
problems.desc:
Print `a` and then `b` using **two** `print` calls, so they appear together on one line with nothing between them, followed by a single new line.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(a), len(b) <= 10^4`
problems.starter:
def same_line(a: str, b: str) -> None:
    pass
hints: Normally each `print` ends with a new line. Here the first one mustn't.
The `end=` option changes what `print` adds at the very end; an empty string `""` adds nothing.
Give the first `print` an empty ending and leave the second one as normal, so the line still ends after `b`.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Stay on the same line:** `print(p, end="")`. The next `print` continues right after it.
**The second print** ends normally with a new line.

problems.title: Echo the Name
problems.desc:
Read one line (a name) with `input()`, then print `Hello NAME`.

**Constraints**
- The input is one line of 1 to 100 characters
hints: `input()` waits for one line of typed text and gives it back as a string. The tests type the name for you.
Store what `input()` returns in a variable, then print a greeting with it.
`print` with two values separated by a comma puts exactly one space between them, which matches `Hello Ada`.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Print two values with a space:** `print("Hello", person)`

problems.title: Add Two Inputs
problems.desc:
Read two whole numbers, one per line, and print their sum.

**Constraints**
- The input is two lines, each a whole number from `-10^7` to `10^7`
hints: Read two lines with two `input()` calls; each one gives you text.
Text doesn't add up like numbers do (`"2" + "3"` is `"23"`), so convert each line with `int(...)` first.
Then print the sum of the two numbers.
problems.solution:
def main() -> None:
    a = int(input())
    b = int(input())
    print(a + b)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Read a line:** `input()` gives the typed text as a string.

problems.title: String Length
problems.desc:
Return how many characters `s` has.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
- `s` can contain any characters, including emoji
hints: You want the number of characters in the text, counting spaces and punctuation too.
The built-in `len(...)` gives the length of a string (and of lists, and more).
Return what `len` gives you for `s`. An empty string has length 0.
problems.solution:
def length(s: str) -> int:
    return len(s)

problems.title: First and Last
problems.desc:
Return the first character of `s` followed by its last character.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: Every character in a string has a position number (an index), starting from 0 for the first character.
Square brackets read one character: `word[0]` is the first. Negative positions count from the end, so `word[-1]` is the last.
Read both characters and join them with `+`. With a one-letter string, the first and last characters are the same letter, so you get it twice.
problems.solution:
def ends(s: str) -> str:
    return s[0] + s[-1]

problems.title: Middle Character
problems.desc:
Return the middle character of `s`, which has an odd length.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
- `len(s) % 2 == 1`
hints: For an odd length like 5, the middle position is 2 (positions 0, 1, **2**, 3, 4).
That middle position is the length divided by 2, using whole-number division `//` so you get an int (indexes must be whole numbers).
Work out the middle index from `len(s)`, then use it inside square brackets.
problems.solution:
def middle(s: str) -> str:
    return s[len(s) // 2]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Middle index:** `len(s) // 2`. Floor division keeps it a whole number.
**Index with an expression:** `word[2 + 1]` works; anything that gives a whole number can go in the brackets.

problems.title: Repeat It
problems.desc:
Return `s` repeated `n` times.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
- `-100 <= n <= 100`
problems.starter:
def repeat(s: str, n: int) -> str:
    pass
hints: Repeating text `n` times is like multiplying it.
In Python, a string times a number repeats it: `"ha" * 2` gives `"haha"`.
Return `s` multiplied by `n`. If `n` is 0 you get an empty string automatically.
problems.solution:
def repeat(s: str, n: int) -> str:
    return s * n

problems.title: First Three
problems.desc:
Return the first three characters of `s` (or all of it, if it's shorter).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: A slice takes a stretch of a string: `text[start:stop]` goes from `start` up to, but not including, `stop`.
Leave out `start` and the slice begins at the very beginning.
Slices never crash when they go past the end; they just stop at the end. So a short string comes back whole.
problems.solution:
def first_three(s: str) -> str:
    return s[:3]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **From the start up to index 3:** `s[:3]`. It's fine if `s` is shorter.

problems.title: Reverse the Text
problems.desc:
Return `s` backwards.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: A slice can have a third number, the step: `text[start:stop:step]`.
A step of `-1` walks backwards through the string.
Leave start and stop empty so the slice covers the whole string, and use a step of -1.
problems.solution:
def reverse(s: str) -> str:
    return s[::-1]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Step of -1:** `s[::-1]` walks the string from the end to the start.

problems.title: Every Other Character
problems.desc:
Return the characters of `s` at positions 0, 2, 4 and so on, as a string.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: You want positions 0, 2, 4, …: start at the beginning and jump 2 each time.
The third slice number is the step size.
Leave start and stop empty (the whole string) and use a step of 2.
problems.solution:
def every_other(s: str) -> str:
    return s[::2]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **A step:** the third number in a slice, `s[::2]`.

problems.title: Drop the Ends
problems.desc:
Return `s` without its first and last characters. If `s` has fewer than 2 characters, return `""`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: You want everything from position 1 up to, but not including, the last character.
`-1` as a slice end means "stop just before the last character".
Slice from 1 to -1. For strings shorter than 2, that slice is already empty, so no `if` is needed.
problems.solution:
def inner(s: str) -> str:
    return s[1:-1]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Stop before the last:** a stop of `-1`.
**Together:** `s[1:-1]`. Slices never raise errors, so short strings just give `""`.

problems.title: Capitalise the First Letter
problems.desc:
Return `s` with only its first character changed to upper case.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: Split the job in two: the first character (made upper case) and everything after it (unchanged).
`.upper()` makes text upper case. A slice like `text[:1]` gives the first character, or an empty string if `text` is empty, so it never crashes.
Join the upper-cased first part and the rest with `+`. Using `s[0]` instead would crash on an empty string.
problems.solution:
def cap_first(s: str) -> str:
    return s[:1].upper() + s[1:]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Glue with a separator:** `", ".join(words)`. The separator goes before `.join`.

problems.title: Read a CSV Line
problems.desc:
Split a comma-separated line into a list of its fields, leaving any spaces as they are. An empty field still counts as a field.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(line) <= 10^4`
hints: Each comma separates two fields, so the line should be cut at every comma.
`.split(",")` cuts at every comma. Unlike `.split()`, it keeps empty fields (that's how `,,` gives `""`).
Return the list `split` gives you. Don't strip the spaces: the task says to keep them.
problems.solution:
def fields(line: str) -> List[str]:
    return line.split(",")

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Split on a separator:** `line.split(",")`. Empty fields are kept.
**Note:** `"".split(",")` is `['']`, a list with one empty string.

problems.title: Last Name First
problems.desc:
Turn `"First Last"` into `"Last, First"`.

**Constraints**
- `3 <= len(name) <= 100`
- `name` is exactly two words with one space between them
hints: Break the name into its two words, then put them back in the other order.
`.split()` gives you a list of two words, and you can unpack it straight into two variables: `a, b = ...`.
Build the result as the last name, then `", "`, then the first name.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Unpack two items into two names:** `leader, ultimate = who.split()`

problems.title: snake_case to camelCase
problems.desc:
Convert `snake_case` to `camelCase`: remove the underscores and capitalise each word after the first.

**Constraints**
- `2 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
- `s` is lowercase letters, digits and underscores
hints: Split the text at the underscores. The first word stays as it is; every word after it gets a capital first letter.
`.split("_")` gives the words. `.capitalize()` makes the first letter upper case and the rest lower.
Keep the first word, capitalise the rest, and glue everything together with `"".join(...)` (join with nothing between).
A single word with no underscores should come back unchanged.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Option B (preview of level 5):** star unpacking, `head, *remainder = [1, 2, 3]`, puts the leftovers in a list.

problems.title: Introduce Someone
problems.desc:
Return `"NAME is AGE years old"`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(name) <= 10^4`
- `-1000 <= age <= 1000`
problems.starter:
def introduce(name: str, age: int) -> str:
    pass
hints: You're building a sentence with two values slotted in.
An f-string (a string with `f` before the opening quote) lets you put values inside curly braces: `f"I am {name}"`.
Write the sentence as an f-string with both values in braces. Numbers are converted to text for you.
problems.solution:
def introduce(name: str, age: int) -> str:
    return f"{name} is {age} years old"

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **f-string:** put `f` before the quotes and the values in braces: `f"{name} is {age} years old"`.
**No `str()` needed:** f-strings convert numbers for you.

problems.title: Two Decimal Places
problems.desc:
Return `x` as text with exactly two decimal places.

**Constraints**
- `x` is an int or a float
- `-10^16 <= x <= 10^16`
hints: You need text with exactly two digits after the point, even for whole numbers (`2` → `"2.00"`).
Inside an f-string's braces you can add a format after a colon. `.2f` means "a float with 2 decimal places".
Put `x` in the braces followed by that format. It rounds for you.
problems.solution:
def money(x: float) -> str:
    return f"{x:.2f}"

tests.note: rounds up to the next whole

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Fixed decimals:** `f"{x:.2f}"`. `.2f` means "a float with 2 decimal places".
**Not the same as `round`:** `round(2, 2)` is `2`, but the format always shows `2.00`.

problems.title: Zero-Padded Number
problems.desc:
Ticket numbers are always 4 digits, padded with zeros. Use the built-in `format` function.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 99999`
hints: The number must always be 4 characters wide, with zeros filling the front.
`format(value, spec)` formats a value using a format spec (the same mini-language as f-strings).
In the spec, `0` means "pad with zeros", `4` is the width and `d` means a whole number. Put those together.
problems.solution:
def ticket(n: int) -> str:
    return format(n, "04d")

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Zero-pad to 4 digits:** the spec `"04d"`. Longer numbers aren't cut off.

problems.title: As a Percentage
problems.desc:
Return `part / whole` as a percentage with one decimal place.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= part, whole <= 10^16`
- `whole != 0`
problems.starter:
def percent(part: int, whole: int) -> str:
    pass
hints: First divide `part` by `whole` to get a fraction like 0.333…
The `%` format type multiplies by 100 and adds a percent sign for you. `.1%` also rounds to one decimal place.
Put the division inside an f-string's braces, followed by the format. Don't multiply by 100 yourself as well.
problems.solution:
def percent(part: int, whole: int) -> str:
    return f"{part / whole:.1%}"

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Percent format:** `.1%` multiplies by 100, shows 1 decimal place and adds `%`.

problems.title: Receipt Line
problems.desc:
Return a 20-character receipt line: the item name left-aligned in 12 characters, then the price right-aligned in 8 characters with 2 decimals.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(item) <= 12`
- `0 <= price <= 99999.99`
problems.starter:
def receipt_line(item: str, price: float) -> str:
    pass
hints: Two fixed-width columns: the name padded to 12 characters on the left, the price padded to 8 on the right.
In an f-string format, `<` means align left and `>` means align right, followed by the width.
For the price, combine right-alignment, width 8 and two decimal places in one format. Put both formatted values next to each other with nothing between them.
problems.solution:
def receipt_line(item: str, price: float) -> str:
    return f"{item:<12}{price:>8.2f}"

problems.title: Character Code
problems.desc:
Return the Unicode code point of the single character `c`.

**Constraints**
- `len(c) == 1`
hints: Every character has a number code (its Unicode code point). For example `A` is 65.
`ord(...)` gives the code of a single character.
Return `ord` of `c`.
problems.solution:
def code(c: str) -> int:
    return ord(c)

problems.title: Next Letter
problems.desc:
Return the letter after `c` in the alphabet, wrapping `"z"` around to `"a"`.

**Constraints**
- `c` is a single lowercase English letter
hints: Turn the letter into a number, add one, and turn it back into a letter. `ord` gives the number and `chr` turns a number back into a character.
To wrap `z` round to `a`, first work out the letter's position from 0 to 25 (its code minus the code of `"a"`).
Add one to that position, use `% 26` so 26 wraps back to 0, then add the code of `"a"` back on and convert with `chr`.
problems.solution:
def next_letter(c: str) -> str:
    return chr((ord(c) - ord("a") + 1) % 26 + ord("a"))

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Letter to 0-25:** a letter's code minus the code of `"a"`.

problems.title: Alphabet Position
problems.desc:
Return the position of letter `c` in the alphabet, starting at 1 and ignoring case.

**Constraints**
- `c` is a single English letter, lowercase or uppercase
hints: Lower-case the letter first, so `A` and `a` give the same answer.
Letters have consecutive codes, so the code of a letter minus the code of `"a"` is its position counting from 0.
Add one, because the alphabet positions here start at 1.
problems.solution:
def position_in_alphabet(c: str) -> int:
    return ord(c.lower()) - ord("a") + 1

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Distance from 'a':** `ord(c) - ord("a")`, then `+ 1` to start counting at 1.

problems.title: Valid PIN
problems.desc:
A PIN is valid if it is exactly 4 or 6 characters long and contains only digits.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(pin) <= 10^4`
hints: Two rules must both hold: the length is 4 or 6, and every character is a digit.
`.isdigit()` is `True` only when the string is non-empty and made only of digits.
Combine the length check (4 *or* 6) and the digit check with `and`. Put brackets round the length check so the `or` is grouped first.
problems.solution:
def valid_pin(pin: str) -> bool:
    return (len(pin) == 4 or len(pin) == 6) and pin.isdigit()

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Is it one of several values?** `x in (1, 2)`
**Brackets around the `or`:** `(a or b) and c`

problems.title: Just Letters
problems.desc:
Return `True` if `s` is non-empty and made only of letters.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: You need to know whether every character is a letter.
`.isalpha()` checks exactly that, and it's `False` for an empty string.
Return the result of calling it on `s`.
problems.solution:
def is_word(s: str) -> bool:
    return s.isalpha()

problems.title: Is It Shouting?
problems.desc:
Return `True` if `s` has at least one letter and all its letters are capitals.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: "Shouting" means there's at least one letter, and none of the letters are lower case. Digits and punctuation don't matter.
`.isupper()` follows exactly those rules: it ignores non-letters but needs at least one capital letter.
Return what `isupper` says. That's why `"123"` is `False`: it has no letters at all.
problems.solution:
def is_shouting(s: str) -> bool:
    return s.isupper()

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **All letters upper case (and at least one letter):** `s.isupper()`. Digits and punctuation are ignored.

problems.title: Show the repr
problems.desc:
Return the `repr` of `s`: the text you'd type to create it, including quotes.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: The "repr" of a value is how you'd write it in code: for text, that includes the quotes.
The built-in `repr(...)` produces it.
Return `repr` of `s`. Notice Python picks the kind of quotes for you.
problems.solution:
def show(s: str) -> str:
    return repr(s)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Programmer's view of a value:** `repr(s)`. Note Python picks double quotes when the text contains a `'`.

problems.title: ASCII-Safe Text
problems.desc:
Return the `ascii` representation of `s`, which escapes every non-ASCII character.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: ASCII is the basic set of English characters. Anything else (like `é` or an emoji) needs to be written as an escape code.
The built-in `ascii(...)` works like `repr`, but escapes every non-ASCII character.
Return `ascii` of `s`.
problems.solution:
def ascii_safe(s: str) -> str:
    return ascii(s)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **repr with escapes:** `ascii(s)` turns `é` into `\xe9` (and wider characters into `\u…`).

problems.title: Hidden Whitespace
problems.desc:
Return `True` if `s` has whitespace at the start or end (a common bug in user input).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: If there's whitespace at either end, removing it changes the text.
`.strip()` returns a copy without whitespace at either end.
Compare the original text with its stripped version: if they're different, there was hidden whitespace.
problems.solution:
def has_hidden(s: str) -> bool:
    return s != s.strip()

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Debugging tip:** `print(repr(s))` would show `'ok '` so you can see the space.

problems.desc:
A command-line tool lists every user on its own line. Write `roll_call(names)` to print each name in order.

An empty list prints nothing.

_This task checks what you print._

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(names) <= 10^4`
- `0 <= len(names[i]) <= 100`
hints: A `for` loop runs its indented lines once for each item in a list.
Inside the loop, the loop variable holds the current item.
Print the loop variable each time round. An empty list prints nothing.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Loop over a list:** `for item in cart:`

problems.title: Add Them Up
problems.desc:
Return the sum of `nums` using a loop (the built-in `sum` comes later in this level).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: Keep a running total that starts at 0, and add each number to it as you go.
`for x in nums:` runs the indented lines once for each item, with `x` set to that item.
Inside the loop, add the current item to the total (`+=` adds to a variable). Return the total *after* the loop finishes, not inside it.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Start a running total:** `partner = 0` before the loop.
**Return after the loop:** `return pattern`, at the function's indentation level.

problems.title: Count the Negatives
problems.desc:
Return how many numbers in `nums` are below zero.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: You're counting, so start a counter at 0.
Loop over the numbers, and use an `if` inside the loop to check whether the current number is below zero.
Only add 1 to the counter when the check passes. Zero isn't negative.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **An `if` inside the loop:** indent it one more level than the `for`.

problems.title: Largest Without max
problems.desc:
Return the largest number in `nums` without using `max`.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: Keep track of the biggest number you've seen so far.
Start with the first item (`nums[0]`) as your best guess, not with 0: if every number is negative, 0 would be wrong.
Loop over every number; whenever one is bigger than your current best, it becomes the new best.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Best so far:** `high_mark = values[0]`. Starting at `0` breaks on all-negative lists.
**Replace when bigger:** `if val > record: record = val`

problems.title: Count a Letter
problems.desc:
Count how many times `letter` appears in `s`, using a loop over the characters.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
- `len(letter) == 1`
problems.starter:
def count_letter(s: str, letter: str) -> int:
    pass
hints: A `for` loop over a string gives you one character at a time.
Start a counter at 0 and compare each character with `letter` using `==`.
Add 1 for each match. Upper and lower case are different characters, so `"A"` doesn't match `"a"`.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Loop over a string:** `for symbol in text:` gives one character at a time.

problems.title: Longest Name Without max
problems.desc:
A table needs to be as wide as its longest name. Write `longest_name(names)` to return the longest name, or the first one if several tie, without using `max`.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(names) <= 10^4`
- `0 <= len(names[i]) <= 100`
hints: Keep track of the best name found so far, starting with the first one.
Compare the lengths with `len(...)`, not the names themselves.
Replace the best only when a name is strictly longer, so ties keep the first one.

problems.title: Print 1 to N
problems.desc:
A progress log prints each step number as it runs. Write `rows(n)` to print the numbers from 1 to `n`, one per line.

If `n` is 0, nothing is printed.

_This task checks what you print._

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 1000`
hints: `range(start, stop)` counts from `start` up to but not including `stop`.
To finish at `n`, the stop has to be one more than `n`.
Print each number the loop gives you.

problems.title: One to N
problems.desc:
Return the list `[1, 2, …, n]` (empty if `n` is 0).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 1000`
hints: `range(start, stop)` counts from `start` up to, but **not including**, `stop`.
To include `n` itself, the stop needs to be one more than `n`.
`range` gives numbers one at a time; wrap it in `list(...)` to get an actual list. When `n` is 0 it's empty automatically.
problems.solution:
def one_to_n(n: int) -> List[int]:
    return list(range(1, n + 1))

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Start and stop:** `range(1, n + 1)`. The `+ 1` is because the stop isn't included.

problems.title: Even Numbers up to N
problems.desc:
Return every even number from 0 up to and including `n`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 1000`
hints: Even numbers go 0, 2, 4, …, which is counting in steps of 2.
`range` takes an optional third number, the step: `range(start, stop, step)`.
Start at 0, step by 2, and make the stop one past `n` so that `n` is included when it's even. Wrap it in `list(...)`.
problems.solution:
def evens(n: int) -> List[int]:
    return list(range(0, n + 1, 2))

problems.title: Countdown
problems.desc:
Return `[n, n-1, …, 1]`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 1000`
hints: Counting down means a step of `-1`.
With a negative step, `range` stops *before* reaching the stop value, just as it does going up.
Start at `n` and stop at 0 so the last number is 1. Wrap it in `list(...)`.
problems.solution:
def countdown(n: int) -> List[int]:
    return list(range(n, 0, -1))

problems.title: Sum of Squares
problems.desc:
Return `1² + 2² + … + n²` using a loop.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 1000`
hints: You need 1×1 + 2×2 + … + n×n: loop over the numbers from 1 to `n`.
`range(1, n + 1)` gives exactly 1 to `n`.
Keep a running total, and add each number multiplied by itself.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Loop over numbers:** `for kk in range(1, num + 1):`

problems.title: Times Table Row
problems.desc:
Print the `n` times table from 1 to 5, one line each, as `1 x n = …`.

**Constraints**
- `-10^16 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: This task checks what you print: five lines, for 1 to 5.
Loop over `range(1, 6)` and print one line per number.
An f-string makes the line easy: put the loop number, the `n` and their product inside braces. Match the spacing exactly: `1 x 3 = 3`.

problems.title: Every Third Item
problems.desc:
A sampling script keeps every third record from a log, starting with the first. Write `every_third(items)` to return the items at positions 0, 3, 6 and so on, using `range` with a step (no slicing).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
hints: You want positions 0, 3, 6, and so on, up to the end of the list.
`range` takes a third number, the step, and the stop can be the list's length.
Loop over those positions and collect the item at each one.

problems.title: Doubling Until a Target
problems.desc:
A cache doubles its capacity every time it fills up, starting from 1 slot. Write `days_to_reach(target)` to return how many doublings it takes to have at least `target` slots.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= target <= 10^16`
hints: You don't know in advance how many doublings it takes, which is exactly when a `while` loop fits.
Keep two numbers: the current size and the number of doublings so far.
While the size is still below the target, double it and count one doubling. A target of 1 needs 0 doublings.

tests.note: just over a power of two

problems.title: Digit Sum
problems.desc:
Return the sum of the digits of `n`, using arithmetic rather than converting to text.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: `% 10` gives the last digit of a number (`123 % 10` is 3), and `// 10` removes the last digit (`123 // 10` is 12).
A `while` loop keeps going as long as its condition is true; here, as long as there are digits left (the number is above 0).
Each time round: add the last digit to a total, then chop it off. When `n` is 0 the total is 0.

problems.title: First Negative
problems.desc:
Return the index of the first negative number, or `-1` if there isn't one. Stop looking as soon as you find it.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: Walk through the positions with a counter that starts at 0.
`break` jumps straight out of the loop, so you can stop the moment you find a negative number.
After the loop, work out whether you stopped early (found one) or ran off the end (none found, so the answer is `-1`).

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Or return early:** `return idx` inside the loop, and `return -1` after it.

problems.title: How Many Halvings
problems.desc:
How many times can you halve `n` (with `//`) before it reaches 0?

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 10^16`
hints: Count how many times you can do `n //= 2` before `n` becomes 0.
A `while` loop with a step counter: keep halving while `n` is above 0, adding 1 each time.
Check the example: 8 → 4 → 2 → 1 → 0 is 4 halvings. Starting at 0, the answer is 0.

tests.note: one below a power of two

problems.title: Skip the Negatives
problems.desc:
Add up the numbers in `nums`, skipping negatives, using `continue`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: Add up the numbers, but leave the negative ones out.
`continue` skips the rest of the loop body for this item and moves straight on to the next one.
At the top of the loop, if the number is negative, `continue`. Otherwise add it to the total.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Then the normal work:** `running_total += v` runs only for items that weren't skipped.

problems.title: First Failed Check
problems.desc:
A CI script runs its checks in order and reports the first one that failed. Write `first_failure(results)` to return the index of the first `"fail"`, or `-1` if every check passed. Use `break` to stop looking once you find it.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(results) <= 10^4`
- Each `results[i]` is `"pass"` or `"fail"`
hints: Start your answer as -1, meaning "not found yet".
Loop with positions (`enumerate`), and when you meet a failure, remember its position.
Then `break` straight away, so a later failure can't overwrite the first one.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Position and item:** `for k, item in enumerate(things):`

problems.title: A List of Placeholders
problems.desc:
A task tracker creates `n` empty slots marked `"pending"` before any work starts. Write `pending(n)` to build that list by appending one `"pending"` at a time in a loop.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= n <= 1000`
hints: Start with an empty list.
Loop `n` times with `range`; the loop variable isn't needed, so `_` is a fine name.
Each time round, `append` one `"pending"`.

problems.title: Add to the End (in place)
problems.desc:
Add `x` to the end of `items`, changing the list itself. Don't return anything.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- `items` and `x` can hold values of any type
problems.starter:
def add_item(items: List[int], x: int) -> None:
    pass
hints: "In place" means changing the list you were given, not making a new one. The function returns nothing.
Lists have a method that adds one item to the end.
Call `append` on `items`. Don't write `items = ...` and don't `return` anything.
problems.solution:
def add_item(items: List[int], x: int) -> None:
    items.append(x)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Nothing to return:** the tests check `items` itself afterwards.

problems.title: Add to the Front (in place)
problems.desc:
Put `x` at the start of `items`, in place.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- `items` and `x` can hold values of any type
problems.starter:
def push_front(items: List[int], x: int) -> None:
    pass
hints: There's no `append` for the front, but there is a method that adds an item at any position.
`.insert(position, item)` puts `item` at that position and shifts everything else along.
Position 0 is the very front.
problems.solution:
def push_front(items: List[int], x: int) -> None:
    items.insert(0, x)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Insert at a position:** `things.insert(0, v)`. Position 0 is the front.

problems.title: Join Two Lists (in place)
problems.desc:
Add every item of `b` to the end of `a`, in place.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(a), len(b) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
problems.starter:
def extend_with(a: List[int], b: List[int]) -> None:
    pass
hints: You want every item of `b` added to the end of `a`, changing `a` itself.
`.append(b)` would add the whole list `b` as one single item. `.extend(b)` adds its items one by one.
Call `extend` on `a`, passing `b`. Don't return anything.
problems.solution:
def extend_with(a: List[int], b: List[int]) -> None:
    a.extend(b)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Compare:** `a.append(b)` would add the whole list `b` as one item.

problems.title: Remove a Value (in place)
problems.desc:
Remove the first `x` from `items`, in place. If `x` isn't there, leave the list alone.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- `items` and `x` can hold values of any type
problems.starter:
def remove_value(items: List[int], x: int) -> None:
    pass
hints: `.remove(x)` deletes the first `x` it finds, but it crashes (raises an error) if `x` isn't in the list.
Check first with `x in items`.
Only call `remove` when the check passes; otherwise do nothing.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Remove the first match:** `things.remove(v)`. It raises `ValueError` if `v` is missing.

problems.title: Take the Last One
problems.desc:
Remove the last item from `items` and return it.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
hints: You need to take the last item out of the list *and* give it back.
`.pop()` does both: it removes the last item and returns it.
Return what `pop` gives you.
problems.solution:
def take_last(items: List[int]) -> int:
    return items.pop()

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Remove and get back the last item:** `items.pop()`

problems.title: Sort in Place
problems.desc:
Sort `items` from largest to smallest, in place.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= items[i] <= 10^16`
hints: Sort the list itself (in place) rather than making a sorted copy.
`.sort()` sorts a list in place, smallest first by default.
Pass `reverse=True` to get largest first. `.sort()` returns `None`, so don't return its result.
problems.solution:
def sort_desc(items: List[int]) -> None:
    items.sort(reverse=True)

problems.title: Position and Count
problems.desc:
Return `[first position of x, how many times x appears]`.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- `x` appears in `items` at least once
problems.starter:
def find_and_count(items: List[int], x: int) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: Two answers: where `x` first appears, and how many times it appears.
`.index(x)` gives the first position; `.count(x)` counts occurrences.
Return both inside a list, position first.
problems.solution:
def find_and_count(items: List[int], x: int) -> List[int]:
    return [items.index(x), items.count(x)]

problems.title: Top Three Without Changing the List
problems.desc:
A leaderboard shows the three best scores, largest first, but the original list is shared with other code and must not change. Write `best_three(scores)` to return a new list of the three largest values (fewer if there aren't three).

`.sort()` would change the list you were given, so copy it first.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(scores) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= scores[i] <= 10^16`
hints: You need a copy so the original isn't sorted too. A full slice makes one.
Sort the copy largest first with `reverse=True`.
Return the first three items with a slice, which is safe for short lists.
problems.solution:
def best_three(scores: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    copy = scores[:]
    copy.sort(reverse=True)
    return copy[:3]

problems.title: First Two Items
problems.desc:
A preview card shows only the first two tags of a post. Write `first_two(rows)` to return the first two items (or fewer, if there aren't two), using a slice.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(rows) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
hints: A slice `xs[a:b]` takes items from position `a` up to but not including `b`.
Leaving `a` out means "from the start".
Slices never crash past the end of a list, so short lists are fine.
problems.solution:
def first_two(rows: List[str]) -> List[str]:
    return rows[:2]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **From the start up to a position:** `xs[:4]`

problems.title: Last N Items
problems.desc:
Return the last `n` items of the list (all of them if `n` is larger).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- `0 <= n <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def last_n(items: List[int], n: int) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: A slice starting `n` places from the end gives the last `n` items.
The start position for the last `n` items is the length minus `n`. Slices that go past the start of the list just begin at the beginning.
Watch out for `n == 0`: a slice starting at `-0` is the same as starting at 0, which gives the *whole* list. Handle 0 separately.
problems.solution:
def last_n(items: List[int], n: int) -> List[int]:
    return items[len(items) - n:] if n else []

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **The usual trick:** `items[-n:]`, but `items[-0:]` is the *whole* list, so handle `n == 0` separately.
**Or compute the start:** `items[max(len(items) - n, 0):]` works for every `n`, including 0.

problems.title: Copy, Then Change
problems.desc:
Make a copy of `items`, set the copy's first item to 0, and return `[items, copy]`. The original must be unchanged.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
hints: If you write `copy = items`, both names point at the **same** list (no copy is made), so changing one changes the other.
A full slice `[:]` makes a real, separate copy of a list.
Copy, change the copy's first item to 0, then return both lists. The original must stay as it was.
problems.solution:
def with_first_zeroed(items: List[int]) -> List[List[int]]:
    copy = items[:]
    copy[0] = 0
    return [items, copy]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Why not `clone_n = elems`?** Both names would point at the same list, so changing one changes "both".

problems.title: Use a slice Object
problems.desc:
Return the part of `items` described by `start`, `stop` and `step`, any of which may be `None` (meaning "use the default"). Use the built-in `slice`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- `start`, `stop` and `step` are each `None` or a whole number
- `step != 0`
problems.starter:
def take(items: List[int], start: Optional[int], stop: Optional[int], step: Optional[int]) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: A slice like `items[1:5:2]` can also be described as an object: `slice(1, 5, 2)`.
`None` in a slice object means "use the default", just like leaving a number out of `a[::]`.
Build a `slice` from the three inputs and use it inside square brackets.
problems.solution:
def take(items: List[int], start: Optional[int], stop: Optional[int], step: Optional[int]) -> List[int]:
    return items[slice(start, stop, step)]

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Build a slice from values:** `slice(start, stop, step)`. `None` means "default", just like leaving a gap in `a[::2]`.

problems.title: Rotate Left
problems.desc:
Move the first `k` items to the end. `k` may be larger than the list, in which case it wraps around.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- `0 <= k <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def rotate_left(items: List[int], k: int) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: Rotating left by `k` = the items from position `k` onward, followed by the first `k` items.
If `k` is bigger than the list, rotating by the length brings you back to the start, so only the remainder matters: `k % len(items)`.
Use two slices and join them with `+`. An empty list needs special care, because `% 0` is an error.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Wrap k:** `cap %= len(things)` (check for an empty list first, or you'll divide by zero).

problems.title: Drop the First and Last
problems.desc:
A CSV export wraps its data with a header row and a footer row. Write `middle(rows)` to return `[the rows without the first and last, how many that is]`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(rows) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
hints: A slice can start at 1 and stop at -1 (just before the last item).
That slice is empty for lists with fewer than 3 items, which is what you want.
Then return the slice together with its length, inside a list.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Position and item together:** `for k, item in enumerate(things):`
**Print two values with a space:** `print(a, b)`

problems.title: Numbered List
problems.desc:
Return each item as `"N. item"`, where `N` is its number, starting at 1.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
hints: You need each item together with its number.
`enumerate(items)` gives `(position, item)` pairs. `start=1` makes the counting begin at 1 instead of 0.
Loop over those pairs, build each string with an f-string (number, dot, space, item) and add it to a result list.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Position and item:** `for kk, val in enumerate(things, from_i=1):`

problems.title: Even Positions
problems.desc:
Return the items at even positions (0, 2, 4, …) using `enumerate`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
hints: You need each item's position to decide whether to keep it.
`for i, x in enumerate(items):` gives the position `i` and the item `x` together.
Keep the item when its position is even (`% 2` leaves 0).

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Position and item:** `for kk, val in enumerate(things):`

problems.title: Add Side by Side
problems.desc:
Return a list where each item is `a[i] + b[i]`. Stop at the end of the shorter list.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(a), len(b) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= a[i], b[i] <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def add_lists(a: List[int], b: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    pass
hints: Add the first items together, then the second items, and so on.
`zip(a, b)` walks both lists side by side, giving pairs `(a item, b item)`, and stops at the shorter list.
Loop over those pairs and add each pair's sum to a result list.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Two lists at once:** `for val, term in zip(p, q):`. It stops at the shorter list.

problems.title: Count Matching Positions
problems.desc:
Count the positions where `a` and `b` have the same character (compare up to the shorter length).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(a), len(b) <= 10^4`
problems.starter:
def matches(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    pass
hints: Compare the two strings position by position.
`zip` pairs up characters from both strings and stops at the shorter one, which is exactly what's asked.
Count the pairs where the two characters are equal. A counter in a loop works, or `sum` over a generator of 1s.
problems.solution:
def matches(a: str, b: str) -> int:
    return sum(1 for x, y in zip(a, b) if x == y)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Walk both strings:** `for item, other in zip(lhs, rhs):`

problems.title: Name and Score
problems.desc:
Return `"NAME: SCORE"` for each pair.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(names) <= 10^4`
- `len(scores) == len(names)`
- `-10^16 <= scores[i] <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def report(names: List[str], scores: List[int]) -> List[str]:
    pass
hints: Each name goes with the score at the same position.
`zip(names, scores)` gives you `(name, score)` pairs.
Turn each pair into `"NAME: SCORE"` with an f-string and collect them in a list.
problems.solution:
def report(names: List[str], scores: List[int]) -> List[str]:
    return [f"{n}: {s}" for n, s in zip(names, scores)]

problems.title: Busiest Day
problems.desc:
A traffic report has the days of the week in one list and the number of site visits on each day in another, in the same order. Write `busiest_day(days, visits)` to return the day with the most visits (the first one if there's a tie).

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(days) <= 10^4`
- `len(visits) == len(days)`
- `-10^16 <= visits[i] <= 10^16`
problems.starter:
def busiest_day(days: List[str], visits: List[int]) -> str:
    pass
hints: `zip(a, b)` pairs each day with its visit count.
Keep the best day and its count so far, starting with the first pair.
Replace them only when a day has strictly more visits, so ties keep the first day.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Walk two lists together:** `for a, b in zip(xs, ys):`

problems.title: Add Up a List
problems.desc:
An invoice totals its line amounts. Write `total(amounts)` to return the sum of the list, using `sum`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(amounts) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= amounts[i] <= 10^16`
hints: Python has a built-in that adds up a whole list.
It returns 0 for an empty list, so there's no special case.
Return its result directly.
problems.solution:
def total(amounts: List[int]) -> int:
    return sum(amounts)

problems.title: Average of a List
problems.desc:
Return the average of `nums`, or `0.0` if the list is empty.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: Average = total ÷ how many numbers there are.
`sum(...)` and `len(...)` give you those two numbers.
An empty list would divide by zero, so return `0.0` for it first.
problems.solution:
def average(nums: List[int]) -> float:
    return sum(nums) / len(nums) if nums else 0.0

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Avoid dividing by zero:** check `if xs` first (an empty list counts as false).

problems.title: Top Three Scores
problems.desc:
Return the three highest scores, highest first (fewer if there aren't three). Don't change the input list.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(scores) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= scores[i] <= 10^16`
hints: Sort the scores from highest to lowest, then take the first three.
`sorted(...)` returns a *new* sorted list and leaves the original alone; `reverse=True` sorts highest first.
A slice of the first three items is safe even when there are fewer than three.
problems.solution:
def top_three(scores: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    return sorted(scores, reverse=True)[:3]

problems.title: Backwards Copy
problems.desc:
Return a new list with the items in reverse order, using the built-in `reversed`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(items) <= 10^4`
- Items can be values of any type
hints: `reversed(items)` walks the list backwards, but it gives you a reversed *view*, not a list.
Wrap it in `list(...)` to turn it into a real new list.
The original list must stay unchanged, so don't call `.reverse()` on it.
problems.solution:
def backwards(items: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    return list(reversed(items))

problems.title: Median
problems.desc:
Return the median of `nums`: the middle value once sorted, or the average of the two middle values if the length is even.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: The median is the middle value of the *sorted* numbers, so sort first (with `sorted`, which doesn't change the input).
The middle index is the length divided by 2 (whole-number division).
Odd length: return the value at the middle. Even length: average the two middle values (the one at the middle index and the one just before it).

problems.title: Spread
problems.desc:
Return the difference between the largest and smallest numbers in `nums`.

**Constraints**
- `1 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: The spread is the gap between the biggest and smallest numbers.
`max(...)` and `min(...)` both work on a whole list.
Subtract the smallest from the largest. A list with one number has a spread of 0.
problems.solution:
def spread(nums: List[int]) -> int:
    return max(nums) - min(nums)

problems.title: Sort Without Changing the Original
problems.desc:
A report shows scores from highest to lowest, and the original list must stay as it is. Write `ranked(scores)` to return a new list sorted largest first, using `sorted`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(scores) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= scores[i] <= 10^16`
hints: `sorted(...)` returns a brand-new sorted list and leaves the original as it was.
By default it sorts smallest first.
Pass `reverse=True` to get largest first.
problems.solution:
def ranked(scores: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    return sorted(scores, reverse=True)

problems.title: Is Any Job Finished?
problems.desc:
A dashboard lights up as soon as at least one background job has finished. Each job is `True` when it's done. Write `any_done(jobs)` using `any`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(jobs) <= 10^4`
- Each `jobs[i]` is `True` or `False`
hints: `any(list)` is `True` when at least one item is true.
It's `False` for an empty list.
Return its result.
problems.solution:
def any_done(jobs: List[bool]) -> bool:
    return any(jobs)

problems.title: No Zeros
problems.desc:
Return `True` if none of the numbers is 0. Use `all` (remember: 0 is falsy).

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: 0 is "falsy" (counts as false), and every other number is "truthy".
`all(...)` is `True` only if every item is truthy.
So passing the list straight to `all` answers the question. An empty list counts as `True`.
problems.solution:
def no_zeros(nums: List[int]) -> bool:
    return all(nums)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **Every item truthy:** `all(nums)`. 0 is the only falsy number.

problems.title: All Positive
problems.desc:
Return `True` if every number is greater than 0.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(nums) <= 10^4`
- `-10^16 <= nums[i] <= 10^16`
hints: For each number, ask "is it greater than 0?"
A generator expression like `(check for x in nums)` produces one `True` or `False` per number.
Pass that to `all(...)`. Zero isn't positive.
problems.solution:
def all_positive(nums: List[int]) -> bool:
    return all(x > 0 for x in nums)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **A condition for every item:** `all(...)` with a generator such as `(w != "" for w in words)`.

problems.title: Has a Digit
problems.desc:
Return `True` if `s` contains at least one digit.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(s) <= 10^4`
hints: You need just one digit anywhere in the string.
`any(...)` is `True` if at least one item is true; `c.isdigit()` tests a single character.
Check each character with `isdigit` inside `any`.
problems.solution:
def has_digit(s: str) -> bool:
    return any(c.isdigit() for c in s)

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **At least one:** `any(...)` with a generator such as `(ch == "!" for ch in text)`.

problems.title: Strong Password
problems.desc:
A password is strong if it has at least 8 characters, at least one digit, at least one upper-case letter, and at least one lower-case letter.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(pw) <= 10^4`
- `pw` is English letters and digits
hints: Four separate rules, and all of them must hold.
The length rule uses `len`. The other three each need "at least one character that…", which is `any(...)` with `isdigit`, `isupper` or `islower`.
Join the four checks with `and`. A long expression can be wrapped in brackets so it can span lines.

grammar.title: Building blocks
items: **At least one passes:** `any(...)` with a generator inside.
**All of them:** join with `and`. Brackets let one expression span several lines.

problems.title: Check Every Label
problems.desc:
Before saving, a form checks that every label is filled in and starts with a capital letter. Write `all_labelled(labels)` to return `True` only if every label is non-empty and its first character is upper case.

An empty list counts as `True`.

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(labels) <= 10^4`
- `0 <= len(labels[i]) <= 100`
hints: Two checks per label: it isn't empty, and its first character is upper case.
Check the empty case first and join the two checks with `and`, so you never read `[0]` of an empty label.
`all(...)` over a generator gives one answer for every label. An empty list counts as `True`.
problems.solution:
def all_labelled(labels: List[str]) -> bool:
    return all(lab != "" and lab[0].isupper() for lab in labels)

problems.title: Print a Grid
problems.desc:
A terminal game draws its map from a grid of single characters. Write `show(grid)` to print each row as one line, with the characters joined together and no spaces.

_This task checks what you print._

**Constraints**
- `0 <= len(grid) <= 10^4`
- `0 <= len(grid[i]) <= 100`
- `len(grid[i][j]) == 1`
hints: Loop over the rows; each row is a list of letters.
`"".join(list)` glues a list of strings together with nothing between them.
Print the joined row each time round.
